newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Unocal free to invest more in Burma.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Unocal free to invest more in Burma.

text.p: The State Department said on Monday it neither approved nor disapproved of a new deal by Unocal Corp, the largest U.S. investor in Burma, to expand its petroleum business there despite official human-rights concerns.
"We don't encourage American investment in Burma," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said. "We don't actively discourage an American company from going in, but we don't encourage it either."
"So I guess it's Unocal's decision if it wants to go in," he added when asked for the U.S. view of the company's decision to expand cooperation with Burma's military rulers.

Unocal announced a deal extending its rights to explore and develop off-shore gas fields on Thursday, the same day the State Department, in its annual human rights survey, said Burma's "severe repression of human rights increased in 1996."

President Bill Clinton in September signed into law a bill authorising a ban on new investment by U.S. companies if "large scale" repression of the democratic opposition worsened in Burma or if Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, the Nobel peace laureate and leader of the opposition National League for Democracy, were harmed, exiled or detained again.

This measure, known as Cohen-Feinstein for its Senate sponsors, "at least presents the possibility of further sanctions, and should the situation warrant it, then the administration has that as an option," Burns told a news briefing.
The United States already maintains many sanctions against Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council, which seized power in 1988 after crushing a pro-democracy uprising.

Unocal spokesman have arranged one-on-one briefings for reporters in Washington this week to explain its Burma involvement, a favourite target of human rights groups, and make the case against further U.S. sanctions.

The El Segundo, California, company is partners with a unit of Total SA of France in the new production-sharing contract with a state-owned Burmese oil and gas company. Unocal and Total are already partners in a $1.2 billion project to pump gas from the giant Yadana field to Thailand.
Unocal is keen to avoid a repeat of Clinton's 1995 decision that forced Conoco Corp. to void a major deal with Iran and barred American companies from investing in Iran.
Conoco's deal was quickly scooped up by Total in the absence of any French government ban on investment in Iran, which the Clinton administration brands the biggest state sponsor of terrorism.
In a speech ready by her husband at American University in Washington last week, Aung San Suu Kyi urged a worldwide boycott of companies doing business in Burma.

"Investment that only goes to enrich an already wealthy elite bent on monopolising both economic and political power cannot contribute toward equality and justice, the foundation stones for a sound democracy," she said. "Please use your liberty to promote ours."
